messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When the chemical plant ignited in 1998, thirty-two-year-old Arthur Vance was already wedged between crumbling scaffolding and roaring flames. The disaster unfolded with terrifying unpredictability; support beams shattered without warning, and the wind shifted the toxic plume across the loading docks just as he was documenting the evacuation. Amid the chaos, he inhaled a sharp, acrid taste of burnt sulfur and melted plastic that coated his tongue, a sensory imprint that would later anchor his memories to a specific, nauseating flavor. The photographs he captured that day—grainy contact sheets of trapped workers and collapsed fire escapes—became the visual anchor of his trauma, freezing the moment in his mind before the smoke even cleared. Now seventy-three, Arthur finds that those very photographs and the unpredictable rhythm of city streets immediately amplify his threat monitoring. When a news broadcast flashes similar footage or he accidentally tastes that same burnt-metal coffee at the diner, his body does not just remember the disaster; it instantly primes him for danger. That sudden spike of alarm causes his eyes to dart toward fire extinguishers, heavy lamps, and protruding tools, which he instinctively catalogues as potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment. Because his body constantly anticipates harm, he has come to believe that if I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, so he rigorously avoids any narrative that touches the past. To manage this crushing weight, he instinctively reaches for his credit card, spending money impulsively to distract or comfort himself from the panic. The relentless threat monitoring has hardened into profound negative appraisals that feed directly back into his memories. His conviction that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again detaches the event from reality, making the story feel so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me. Yet each time the memory replay plays over and over, it floods his nervous system, so he finds himself listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home, unable to relax even when he knows he is in a safe place. The relentless memory replay plays over and over, each loop reinforcing the negative appraisal that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. The memory replay plays over and over, actively pulling up related photos on his old camera roll and forcing that specific taste associated with the event onto his tongue. His avoidance strategies have created a self-reinforcing loop that dominates his daily life in his small, book-cluttered apartment. When he relives the event, feeling like it is happening right now, he instinctively freezes completely when threatened. His habit of always sitting with back against a wall prevents processing, which allows the memory replay to play over and over without fading. His compulsive spending to distract or comfort himself confirms his dread that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, as if he is just purchasing time to survive. The freeze response prevents him from habituating to sensory cues, so the specific taste associated with the event and visual photos retain their full, shocking power. His heightened threat state makes ordinary unpredictability feel catastrophic, so unpredictable situations become potent triggers that bypass his defenses. The constant dread of danger around him solidifies his negative appraisal that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. The pervasive threat monitoring exhausts his coping reserves, pushing him toward compulsive spending to distract or comfort himself and freezing completely when threatened. Sitting with back against a wall never truly lowers his baseline arousal, so he remains unable to relax even when he knows he is in a safe place. His inability to relax ensures his nervous system stays in high gear, which in turn fuels the relentless memory replay that plays over and over without fading. After decades of this tightening cycle, Arthur finally booked an appointment when a sudden power outage triggered a full freeze episode, leaving him unable to navigate his own kitchen or call for help. He sits now in the therapist’s office, hands folded tightly over his knees, terrified that speaking about the disaster will permanently shatter his composure. Yet beneath the fear, a fragile hope remains that he might finally learn how to step out of the periphery, sit without checking the walls, and remember that the smoke has long since cleared.
